messages.body_plain:
Hi,
if you have data in HBase on which you would like to run mapreduce jobs written in R with rmr, please get in touch with me. The hbase-io branch adds an input format called hbase that allows you to do just that and I've just taken it through the first small test runs. This is way not ready for production, but we need your help to further develop this feature. What are you trying to do with the data and how is it serialized? The corresponding output format is in the works but is a little further down the road. Thanks

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#421] Memory limitations of RHadoop?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your replies, Antonio! They are very helpful.

On Friday, November 30, 2012 11:01:51 AM UTC-6, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:

> RHadoop is a collection of three packages. rhdfs and rhbase run within a single R instance and load data in memory directly, I would say they are mostly subject to memory limitations (I say mostly because you can probably code your way around it by reading subsets of the data). rmr instead adopts the mapreduce model, therefore loads into memory only a subset of the data by default. You can still run into memory problems with very large records or if you have a small set of keys in the reduce phase but at least you have a powerful tool to address the problem. It's  no magic bullet, algorithms still need to be designed by humans using their intellect.
>
>
> Antonio

messages.body_plain:
It could be an issue with the size of the input data or the configuration of your hadoop cluster. Additionally it could be that some nodes are misconfigured and fail and all the data has to go through one or few nodes that are properly configured in additional attempts. It also helps if the data is partitioned in advance, which you can achieve with the function scatter.  I hope this helps

Antonio

mapreduce(scatter(to.dfs(1:10^6))

I would start here: hadoop.apache.org/docs/stable/ <http://apache.org/docs/stable/>cluster_setup.html

messages.body_plain:
We are firming up plans for rmr 2.1 and your input would be valuable. If you have any features that you would like to see developed, whether already listed in the issue tracker or not, and if you have some reasonable use cases that support introducing those features; or if you have some use cases that are not particularly well supported, that require workarounds or inelegant code or that appear to run excessively slowly, even if you don't have a clear idea of what changes in rmr could address those situations, this is a good time to come forward. Keep in mind this is a minor version, therefore, following the definitions of Semantic Versioning <http://semver.org>, we are going to delay any non-backward compatible changes. That doesn't mean we can't discuss more long term changes, just don't be disappointed if they have to wait until 3.0. If you check the issue tracker you can see that some issues are already associated with the 2.1 milestone, those are completely tentative and can be changed. Thanks

Not that I am aware of.

>
> should they be installed at the same time that rmr2 is installed or can in be done afterwards/before?

Besides rmr2 dependendcies, they can be installed afterwards.

>
> can it even be left as late as once ssh'ing into the jobtracker node, and in an R environment?

Since you need to install, in the general case, on all nodes, ssh is not a very scalable way of doing it.

>
> could it be part of the the function that is being called in which it also calls for the libraries to be installed/loaded if not already loaded?

Loading is automatic. that is if you write

library(MASS)

mapreduce(input, map = function(k,v) rlm ...

rlm will be available to the map function as long as MASS was installed on the cluster. We have some development going on to weaken the latter requirement.

> also with regard to data that the function calls, the main input obviously needs to be converted using the to.dfs function,

To.dfs is only to create examples, debugging, learning etc. It can not create in a scalable way the amounts of data Hadoop exists to process. So typically the input of a mapreduce call is an HDFS file that was created by some other mean, for instance another mapreduce job. rmr offers the ability to read a number of formats or to define your own format.

> but what about other objects of data that it might refer to? how is that dealt with? i.e. if a map reduce calls two or more objects...do they need to all be converted using to.dfs? and how would each object be incorporated into the mapreduce function?

If they are in memory  they can simply be referred to

y = 1

mapreduce(input, function(k,x) x + y)

just works.

If they are too large for this approach, you can give mapreduce multiple inputs

mapreduce(c(input1, input2), ...

Since the two inputs are merged in an arbitrary order, you may want to consider the function equijoin, which uses this approach to implement a limited version of a relational  join.

Antonio

>
>
> That's how we do it but it works only for a whirr cluster. We include sample whirr files (config and scripts) in the source package, but they have fallen behind as far as being up to date with the latest RHadoop and whirr, something we need to fix.
>
> > >
> > > >

> > > Loading is automatic. that is if you write

> > > library(MASS)
> > >

> > >

> > >
> > > To.dfs is only to create examples, debugging, learning etc. It can not create in a scalable way the amounts of data Hadoop exists to process. > >
> > if for example you wanted to apply a function on an xts object over time using evenly spaced intervals, say for example the last 10 days standard deviation every day (kinda like using a moving window), using the hadoop cluster method, what would be the best Rhadoop/rmr2 way of doing this? >

I am aware that standard deviation is a sub-second calculation...the function i intend to use instead of standard deviation takes about 3-10 minutes to carry out each time it is called, and would like to call it over 10000 times, i.e 10000 days of data. which is about 20 days or longer worth of calculations, something i would rather not do...and thus have looked into RHadoop to do that to split the process up into lots of small parts over many machines....

>
> Antonio
>
>

> > require(xts)
> > n <- 10000

> > window.length <- 10
> >
> > require(rmr2)
> > sd.vals <- values(

> > mapreduce(
> > input=scatter(
> > to.dfs(

> > )),

> > keyval(k,lapply(X=v, function(x){
> > sd(
> > as.numeric(
> > y[c(x:(x+(window.length-1)))]
> > ))})),
> > })))

> > >

> > > just works.

> > >

> > >
> > >

I'm running CDH4 under Cygwin on Windows just fine.  I've run apache hadoop in the past but needed to fixup the hadoop and hbase scripts for windows paths.  There's code in there for cygwin but since it's not much used, it's sometimes out of date.  I don't generally run hadoop services on Windows because we have several linux clusters but I do develop for Hadoop/HBase almost exclusively from my windows machine by connecting to the cluster services.

Once I hacked hdfs.init() to handle building the classpath correctly for windows, it worked perfectly well.

I do have a problem with rhbase hanging but it compiles without problem.  It appears the hanging is within boost when it tries to initialize the connection.  I'm guessing it has to do with the firewall on windows but I haven't dug deeper to see for sure.  I am running the thrift server on my Windows box and I can loop back through it from a linux instance of R where rhbase is working properly.

I may be wrong, but I see no fundamental reason why rmr shouldn't work as well.  I did dig deeper and the compilation problems are an issue with Rcpp and not rmr itself.  Moving my R installation to a path without spaces allowed the build to go further but then I ran into another compile time issue that looks to be Rcpp not doing the right thing under windows.

Since I'm still in the evaluation phase, I punted and moved to running under Virtualbox...which is cumbersome but works well enough.  It's possible that if we decide to adopt R I'll be coming back to these issues but for now, I can run well enough to evaluate what we'd like to see.

Thank you for your help in this!

Brian
